passage: Looking back on Hanoi, I think the best thing I did was stubborn and boring. I'm Pranav, and on our last evening there, Farida and I had to find the station for the night train to Hue. A man on a scooter pulled up beside us. "Station closed today! I take you to the other station, very fast." He was friendly and completely sure. I thanked him and kept walking. At a pharmacy I showed the woman at the counter our ticket; she pointed straight ahead. "Ten minutes. Open." Two streets on, I asked a hotel receptionist the same question and got the same answer. Two against one. All the while, my passport sat in a pouch under my shirt, and our backpacks were on our fronts through the crowded market street. The station was open, of course. On the train Farida said, "You didn't trust him at all." I said, "I trusted him a third."

qa.q: Where did Pranav first ask for directions after the scooter man?
qa.a: At a pharmacy, from the woman at the counter.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when the scooter man insisted the station was closed?
qa.a: Pranav felt wary but calm, polite enough to thank him while quietly doubting such a sure and helpful stranger.

qa.q: Why did asking two more people work better than arguing with the scooter man?
qa.a: Two separate locals giving the same answer outweighed one stranger with something to gain, so Pranav could just keep walking.

qa.q: How might Farida have seen Pranav's checking?
qa.a: Farida seems amused and a little impressed, noticing that Pranav didn't take the friendly man at his word.

grounding: Illustrates a traveller who asks several people, checks their answers against each other and keeps valuables close, avoiding an opportunist.

passage:
After-school care note, Thursday.
Maria found the broken wind-up car in the toy box and asked to "see its insides". I gave her a small screwdriver and a tray. She took out four tiny screws, lifted the shell and gasped. "It's all little wheels with teeth!" She turned the key and watched the gears spin, laughing. Then she pulled the spring out, and it uncoiled with a ping across the table. Nothing would fit back after that. Her face crumpled. The car was broken anyway, so I asked what the spring had been doing. "It pushes the teeth wheels round." Next week I'll bring an old kitchen timer, and Irawati from the older group will show her how to photograph each step so things can go back.

qa.q: How many screws did Maria take out of the car?
qa.a: Four tiny screws.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she lifted the shell, and then when nothing fitted back?
qa.a: She was delighted and amazed at the "wheels with teeth", then briefly upset and disappointed when the spring flew out and it wouldn't go back together.

qa.q: What did the care worker do that made the tinkering useful?
qa.a: Gave her a proper small screwdriver and a tray, stayed with her, and asked what the spring had been doing, turning the mess into understanding.

qa.q: How might Irawati's photo idea help Maria next time?
qa.a: Photographing each step gives Maria a record of the order, so her curiosity can end with the object back together instead of in pieces.

grounding: Shows a child who opens an old toy to see how it works, is thrilled by the gears but can't reassemble it, and gains from supervised tinkering with safe tools.

subtype: Fixing something with a family member [Actor]
passage:
Uma: coming to the library at 5?
Rehana: can't, fixing the front door lock with Nana 🔧
Uma: since when do you fix locks
Rehana: since today apparently
Rehana: it kept sticking. Nana took it apart on newspaper and made me lay out every piece in order, so we'd know how it goes back
Rehana: inside was full of old grease and dust. he said new oil on old dirt just makes paste, so we cleaned it first with an old toothbrush
Uma: that's actually cool
Rehana: then pencil lead dust in the keyhole instead of oil. he says oil pulls in more dust
Rehana: [photo]
Rehana: it clicks now!! smooth like butter
Uma: ok engineer 😄
Rehana: nana let me put it back together myself. he only pointed twice
Rehana: I feel weirdly proud of a lock

qa.q: What did Rehana and Nana use to clean the inside of the lock?
qa.a: An old toothbrush.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel after the lock starts clicking?
qa.a: Rehana feels proud, even "weirdly proud of a lock", and excited enough to send a photo.

qa.q: What did Nana do that helped Rehana really learn?
qa.a: He explained why at each step, like why oil on old dirt makes paste, and let Rehana reassemble it, pointing only twice.

qa.q: How might Nana feel watching Rehana put the lock back together?
qa.a: Nana is probably pleased and quietly proud, passing on his know-how and seeing Rehana manage it almost alone.

passage:
Saturday: Nirmala watched a video twice, then replaced the frayed brake cable on her bicycle in the hostel parking lot. When she squeezed the lever and the wheel stopped dead, she did a small dance. She sent a photo to everyone.
Thursday: The washing machine in her rented flat wouldn't drain. Another video, another confident presenter. She unscrewed the back panel, disconnected a hose, and grey water poured across the floor. The pump wouldn't come out; the video's machine had a clip hers didn't. She sat among wet towels, dismayed, the panel half off.
The next Monday: Chetan, the technician, fixed it in twenty minutes with a special tool, showed her the clip, and gently said, "Anything with water connections or wiring, call someone." That night Nirmala made a list on her phone: "Videos: bike, shelves, curtain rails. Call someone: electrics, gas, anything that floods."

qa.q: What did Nirmala replace on Saturday?
qa.a: The frayed brake cable on her bicycle.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel on Thursday among the wet towels?
qa.a: She was dismayed and deflated, a big change from Saturday's pride, with the pump stuck and water on the floor.

qa.q: How does Nirmala's list help her decide which repairs to try?
qa.a: It separates simple jobs a video can guide, like the bike or shelves, from ones with water or wiring where a professional is the safer choice.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Nirmala's attempt?
qa.a: Chetan seems patient rather than scornful, showing her the clip and gently pointing out which jobs to leave to a technician.

grounding: Shows a young adult proud of a video-guided repair that works and dismayed by one that fails, learning which jobs need a professional.

passage: "Vandana, you remember the night you found me on the bedroom floor holding my wrist? I never told you all of it. I'm Arnab. I've changed a plug top, I once fitted a doorbell, and I thought that made me an electrician. The socket by the bed was loose and sparking. The electrician couldn't come till Monday, and I thought, why wait? I flicked off the switch for that socket, didn't touch the main board, and opened the plate. My screwdriver brushed a wire, and a jolt went up my arm and threw my hand back. I heard myself shout. You ran in and switched off the main before you even asked what happened. I was angry, first at the builder, then at the socket, and only much later at myself, which is where it belonged. The electrician came on Monday and said, 'Never with the power on.' Now anything behind a wall plate is his job, not mine."

qa.q: What did Vandana do on running in?
qa.a: Vandana switched off the main before even asking what happened.

qa.q: What did Arnab feel after the shock?
qa.a: Arnab felt shaken and angry, first blaming the builder and the socket, and only later seeing that the real fault was Arnab's own overconfidence.

qa.q: What should Arnab have done when the socket started sparking?
qa.a: Left it switched off and unused until the electrician came on Monday, since a loose, sparking socket is a job for a licensed person.

qa.q: What might that night have been like for Vandana?
qa.a: Vandana probably heard the shout and felt frightened, acting fast to cut the power before knowing how badly Arnab was hurt.

grounding: Shows an adult whose small wiring successes breed overconfidence, who works on a socket without switching off the main, and learns such jobs belong to a licensed electrician.

passage:
Dear Francis,
I wanted to thank you properly, because on Saturday I was too flustered to.
When the fridge stopped cooling, the first technician spent five minutes behind it and announced that the compressor was finished and had to be replaced that day, at a price that made me sit down. He used words I didn't understand. I felt stupid and cornered. I nearly said yes just to make the feeling stop.
Then I remembered my neighbour's advice and asked him to show me the fault. He waved at the back and said, "It's inside, madam, you won't see." That made me uneasy enough to say I'd think about it.
You came the next morning, showed me the fan at the back jammed with dust and a bit of plastic, cleaned it, and let me feel the cold air come back. You even said the compressor sounded healthy.
Your number is now on the fridge.
Aditi

qa.q: What did Francis find jamming the fan at the back of the fridge?
qa.a: Dust and a bit of plastic.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel while the first technician talked?
qa.a: Aditi felt stupid, cornered and helpless, so much that she nearly agreed just to end the feeling.

qa.q: Which step protected Aditi from a needless repair?
qa.a: Asking the first technician to show the fault, and then getting a second opinion when he wouldn't, which revealed a jammed fan instead of a dead compressor.

qa.q: How might Francis see a customer who asks to be shown the fault?
qa.a: Francis seems to welcome it, showing the fan and even the healthy compressor, which suggests an honest worker is glad to be checked.

grounding: Shows a householder who feels helpless before a technician's unverifiable diagnosis and price, and is protected by asking to see the fault and getting a second opinion.

passage:
Sunday, 2 March
First Sunday of the month, so maintenance hour. Oiled the cycle chain and pumped both tyres. Pulled a horrible clump of hair out of the bathroom drain before it could block. Tightened the loose wardrobe hinge with the small cross-head screwdriver; took two minutes because I knew which drawer it lives in.
Yusuf came in holding a butter knife, trying to open the doorbell's battery cover. I handed him the tiny flat-head from the tool box instead. He laughed: "You have a screwdriver for everything." Then he told me that in his last flat he used pliers on a tap nut and cracked it, and the plumber took a whole morning to fix it.
One box, labelled, in the same cupboard. A handful of small jobs a month. I haven't had to call anyone out since we moved in, and I don't lie awake wondering what's about to break.
Santosh

qa.q: What was Yusuf using to try to open the doorbell's battery cover?
qa.a: A butter knife.

qa.q: How does Santosh feel about the state of the flat?
qa.a: Santosh feels calm and settled, not lying awake wondering what will break next.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's cracked tap nut show about using the wrong tool?
qa.a: Using pliers on a tap nut turned a small job into a broken part and a whole morning for the plumber, which the right tool would have avoided.

qa.q: How does Yusuf react to Santosh's tool box?
qa.a: Yusuf is amused and a little impressed, laughing that Santosh has a screwdriver for everything, perhaps remembering the cracked tap with regret.

grounding: Illustrates a person who keeps labelled tools in one place, uses the right tool for each job and does small monthly maintenance before things fail.

subtype: Pocket money and spending at once [Actor]
passage: I'm Kunal. Every Sunday Nani gives me twenty rupees. Last month I spent it the same day, every time: an orange ice lolly, a packet of stickers, once a plastic whistle that broke by Tuesday. Then came Sankranti. Akash had saved his for four weeks and bought a big red kite and a whole roll of string. On the terrace everyone was flying theirs. I had nothing, only a racing-car sticker on my water bottle. Akash let me hold his string for a while, but it wasn't the same. That night I told Nani, "I want a kite like Akash's next year." Nani said, "Then we'll make a jar." The jar is on my shelf now, with sixty rupees in it. I look at it more than I looked at lollies.

qa.q: How much money is in Kunal's jar now?
qa.a: Sixty rupees.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel on the terrace at Sankranti?
qa.a: Kunal felt left out and envious, holding Akash's string but knowing it wasn't the same as having a kite.

qa.q: What choice is helping Kunal work towards the kite?
qa.a: Deciding with Nani to keep the Sunday money in a jar for the kite, so the bigger wish can grow instead of going on lollies.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt letting Kunal hold the string?
qa.a: Akash was probably kind and a bit proud of the kite, happy to share it for a while.

grounding: Shows a child who spends pocket money the same day and then wants something bigger, and feels the difference between a wish now and a wish later.

passage: "Hemant, you just paid for three things in five minutes and didn't look at one of them. Sit. Your Seema bua did the same at fifteen, the year my father linked my first payment app to his account. Samosa at the canteen: tap. A game pass: tap. My share of a birthday gift: tap. A second samosa, why not: tap. It never felt like money. No notes leaving my hand, no coins getting fewer. Then at the end of the month my father sat me down with his phone and scrolled. Forty-one payments. My face went hot. I remembered maybe ten of them. I wasn't greedy, beta. I just couldn't feel it. So I bought a thin notebook, and after every tap I wrote down the thing and the amount. After a week, the notebook made me pause before tapping. That little pause was the whole trick."

qa.q: How many payments did young Seema's father find at the end of the month?
qa.a: Forty-one payments.

qa.q: How did young Seema feel as her father scrolled through the payments?
qa.a: She was shocked and embarrassed, her face going hot, because she remembered only about ten of them.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Seema's story?
qa.a: Buying the thin notebook and writing down every payment, which brought back the pause that tapping had taken away.

qa.q: How might Seema's father have felt scrolling through the month with her?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and concerned, but he chose to sit down and show her calmly rather than just scold.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose first payment app makes spending feel like nothing, until tracking each payment restores the sense of money leaving.

passage: Dhruv was minding his father's fertiliser shop in the village after school when the phone buzzed. A man said he was a trader from the next taluka. "I'm sending payment for ten bags. Just approve the request on your app, quickly, my tempo is leaving." A request popped up. Dhruv looked closer. It didn't say receive. It said Pay, and it wanted his PIN. "If you're paying me, why do I enter my PIN?" The man's voice went hard. "Don't waste my time! Approve it now." The hurry made Dhruv's neck prickle. He declined the request and said, "My father will call you back." Then he phoned Tanvir chacha at the mandi. His uncle listened and said, "Good. That was a trap. Nobody sends you money by asking for your PIN. Block the number." When his father came home, Dhruv showed him the screenshot, and his father patted his shoulder twice.

qa.q: What did the request on the app actually say?
qa.a: It said Pay, and it wanted his PIN.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when the caller's voice went hard?
qa.a: He was suspicious and uneasy, his neck prickling at the pressure to hurry.

qa.q: Which of Dhruv's steps defeated the trap, and why?
qa.a: He paused to read the request, refused to enter his PIN, declined it and checked with his uncle, because the scam depended on him acting in a rush.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's father feel seeing the screenshot?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and proud, patting Dhruv's shoulder for handling the shop's money carefully.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who pauses under pressure, refuses an unexpected payment request and never shares his PIN, and checks with a trusted adult.
